intro: Money touches almost every choice you make. You earn it at a first job. You decide what to spend and what to save. One day you may borrow for a car, school or a home. This unit is about your own money: how to earn it, plan it, grow it and protect it.

You will read a pay stub and see why the number at the bottom is smaller. You will build a budget and watch compound interest grow a small pile of savings. You will learn what APR and a credit score mean. You will also learn to spot scams and read the fine print before you sign.

By the end, you will be able to plan a month of spending and saving with real math. You will compare the true cost of two deals. You will explain when borrowing helps and when it hurts. These are skills you will use for the rest of your life.
bigQuestion: How can you earn, plan, save, borrow and protect money so that it works for you now and later?

timeline.t: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations says saving builds a nation's capital
The Federal Reserve Act creates the Federal Reserve, with a Reserve Bank in Chicago
Congress creates the FDIC to insure bank deposits after many banks fail
The Social Security Act passes; payroll taxes later fund it
The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to show the cost of credit
The Fair Credit Reporting Act gives people rights over their credit reports
The FICO credit score is introduced for general use
The Credit CARD Act adds new rules for credit card companies
Congress creates the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau

words.d: the full amount you earn before anything is taken out
the amount you receive after taxes and deductions
a plan that shows expected income, spending and saving
the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice
money saved only for unexpected costs
interest paid on the principal and on interest already earned
an agreement to get money or goods now and pay later
annual percentage rate; the yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percent
a number that shows how likely a person is to repay debts
a fake message that tries to get private information
the regular amount paid for insurance
the cost for one unit, such as one ounce

test.q: Gross pay is $700. Deductions are $105. What is net pay?
Using 50/30/20, how much of $2,200 goes to savings?
$500 at 4% simple interest for 3 years earns how much interest?
$1,000 at 10% compounded yearly. How much after 2 years?
You pick a job over a summer camp. The camp was your next-best choice. What is the opportunity cost?
test.why: Opportunity cost is the next-best choice given up.

test.q: Which is the biggest part of a FICO score?
A credit card APR is 12%. About what is the monthly rate?
At 9% a year, about how long until money doubles?

test.why: A credit card is a loan you must repay.

test.q: A repair costs $1,200. The deductible is $250. What does insurance pay?
A 24-ounce box costs $4.80. What is the unit price?
An email asks you to confirm your password by clicking a link. What should you do?
choices: Go to the company's site yourself instead of clicking
Send it to a friend to check
test.why: This is likely phishing. Use a trusted route instead.

test.q: How much does the FDIC insure per depositor, per bank, for each account type?
A phone costs $40 a month for 24 months. What is the total?
Why might a longer loan cost more even with a smaller payment?
choices: Interest is paid for more months
test.why: More months of borrowing means more interest in total.

write.prompt: Priya can pay $999 for a phone now from savings, or $35 a month for 36 months with a $15 fee (example amounts). Her emergency fund has $1,200. Decide which plan is better for her. Use the numbers and name the trade-offs.
tips: Find the total cost of each plan.
Name the opportunity cost of using savings.
Say what happens to her emergency fund in each plan.
Name one question she should ask before signing.
State your choice and the main reason.
